title: Adrenal Crisis
summary: Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately with parenteral hydrocortisone and isotonic saline; obtain diagnostic blood samples first only if this does not delay therapy. Continue stress-dose glucocorticoid replacement, correct hypoglycemia and electrolyte abnormalities, identify the precipitant, and transition only after hemodynamic and clinical stabilization.
seoDescription: Physician guide to immediate adrenal crisis treatment: hydrocortisone dosing, saline resuscitation, diagnostic sampling, monitoring, and transition to oral therapy.
clinicalQuestion: How should physicians recognize, stabilize, investigate, and transition adults and children with suspected adrenal crisis?
keyTakeaways: For suspected adrenal crisis, administer parenteral hydrocortisone immediately; do not delay treatment for diagnostic testing. [14][16][17]
In adults, use hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM initially, then 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours. [14][15]
Give 0.9% sodium chloride and continue intravenous fluid according to hemodynamic parameters and electrolyte status until hemodynamic stability is achieved. [17]
Before the first glucocorticoid dose, collect cortisol and ACTH plus glucose and electrolytes when feasible without postponing resuscitation. [1][2]
Do not give mineralocorticoid replacement while hydrocortisone exceeds 50 mg per 24 hours. [3]

sections.heading: Give hydrocortisone immediately when adrenal crisis is suspected
sections.intro: Clinical suspicion is sufficient to begin emergency treatment.
paragraphs: Treat suspected adrenal crisis as a time-critical glucocorticoid emergency. Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately in adults, then arrange emergency transport or inpatient management; guidance emphasizes that emergency hydrocortisone has no overdose risk in this setting. [14][16][17]

Establish intravenous access, initiate cardiac monitoring, and assess blood pressure, mental status, serum glucose, volume status, and electrolytes while hydrocortisone is being administered. Hypoglycemia, hypotension, and dehydration require concurrent correction rather than sequential management. [1][15]

If presentation is a new suspected adrenal insufficiency, draw diagnostic samples before hydrocortisone only when this can be done immediately. A delay in glucocorticoid treatment to obtain laboratory results is inappropriate in an unstable patient. [1][2][16]
bullets: Initial adult glucocorticoid: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM. [14][15]
Immediate supportive priorities: hypotension, dehydration, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte abnormalities. [1][17]
Disposition: transport to hospital and involve an endocrine team during admission. [17]

sections.heading: Resuscitate with isotonic saline and correct metabolic complications
sections.intro: Hydrocortisone does not replace volume or glucose resuscitation.
paragraphs: Start 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously and titrate ongoing infusion to hemodynamic parameters and electrolyte status until the patient is hemodynamically stable. Continue frequent reassessment of blood pressure, perfusion, mental status, urine output, sodium, potassium, and glucose during early treatment. [17]

Measure and treat hypoglycemia at presentation, especially in children and in patients with impaired consciousness, seizures, or poor oral intake. Hydrocortisone, volume replacement, and glucose correction should proceed concurrently. [1][2]

Continue parenteral stress-dose hydrocortisone during the acute phase. Once the patient is clinically stable and the underlying trigger has resolved or is controlled, transition to at least 40 mg/day oral hydrocortisone in 2 to 4 divided doses, or at least 10 mg/day oral prednisolone in 1 to 2 divided doses, until recovery is established. [17]
bullets: Continue IV 0.9% sodium chloride until hemodynamic stability, guided by vital signs and electrolytes. [17]
Recheck glucose and treat hypoglycemia during the initial resuscitation period. [1][2]
Do not transition from parenteral therapy solely because laboratory abnormalities improve; require clinical and hemodynamic stability. [17]

table.caption: Acute stabilization priorities and treatment endpoints. [1][17]
rows: Hypotension or dehydration
Administer IV 0.9% sodium chloride and adjust infusion to hemodynamics and electrolytes. [17]
Hemodynamic stability. [17]
Hypoglycemia
Measure glucose and treat hypoglycemia during emergency management. [1][2]
Correction of hypoglycemia with ongoing clinical reassessment. [1]
Ongoing cortisol deficiency
Continue 200 mg hydrocortisone over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours in adults. [14][15]
Clinical stability and ability to transition to oral glucocorticoid therapy. [17]

sections.heading: Obtain a pre-treatment adrenal evaluation when feasible
sections.intro: Preserve diagnostic information without compromising emergency therapy.
paragraphs: For a first presentation of suspected adrenal insufficiency or crisis, obtain serum cortisol and plasma ACTH before hydrocortisone when feasible. Add serum glucose, urea and electrolytes, renin, aldosterone, and—when congenital adrenal hyperplasia is in the differential—17-hydroxyprogesterone and urine steroid profile. [1][2]

The acute sample supports later classification but should not be used to defer resuscitation. Elevated endogenous ACTH with impaired adrenal reserve supports primary adrenal insufficiency, whereas the cosyntropin response alone has limited sensitivity for secondary adrenal insufficiency, particularly with recent-onset ACTH deficiency. [23][11]

After stabilization, use a cosyntropin stimulation test when basal cortisol is indeterminate, commonly 5–10 micrograms/dL. Obtain baseline, 30-minute, and 60-minute cortisol values, and interpret the peak using the performing laboratory's assay-specific cutoff. [22][23]
bullets: Document whether cortisol was collected before or after hydrocortisone, because exogenous glucocorticoid exposure can compromise subsequent interpretation. [1][2]
Request the cortisol assay method and the laboratory-specific diagnostic threshold with the cosyntropin result. [22][23]
Consider recent pituitary injury, pituitary apoplexy, or pituitary surgery if a normal cosyntropin response conflicts with high clinical suspicion for new central ACTH deficiency. [11]

subsections.heading: Cosyntropin interpretation after recovery
paragraphs: A historical peak cortisol threshold below 18 micrograms/dL at 30 or 60 minutes after cosyntropin is consistent with adrenocortical insufficiency, but newer assays and LC-MS/MS require lower assay-specific cutoffs. LC-MS/MS thresholds reported in one reference are approximately 412 nmol/L at 30 minutes and 485 nmol/L at 60 minutes. [22][23]

For the Abbott Architect assay, a 60-minute cortisol threshold of 14.6 micrograms/dL has been proposed; applying the historical 18 micrograms/dL threshold to newer assays can increase false-positive diagnoses. [9][10]
bullets: Report baseline, 30-minute, and 60-minute cortisol values, the peak value, assay method, and assay-specific cutoff. [22]
Do not generalize an Abbott Architect cutoff to a different assay platform. [9][10][22]

table.caption: Post-stabilization cortisol testing decisions. [9][10][11][22][23]
rows: Indeterminate early-morning cortisol, typically 5–10 micrograms/dL
Cosyntropin testing is most useful in this range. [22][23]
Measure baseline, 30-minute, and 60-minute cortisol and use the assay-specific peak cutoff. [22]
Historical immunoassay interpretation
Peak cortisol below 18 micrograms/dL at 30 or 60 minutes is historically consistent with insufficiency. [22][23]
Verify whether the local assay requires a lower validated cutoff. [9][10][22]
Recent central ACTH deficiency
Adrenal responsiveness may remain preserved, producing a normal cosyntropin response. [11]
Do not exclude central adrenal insufficiency on cosyntropin response alone when clinical timing is compatible. [11][23]

sections.heading: Step down stress dosing and address mineralocorticoid replacement
sections.intro: Maintain stress coverage until recovery, then return to individualized replacement.
paragraphs: Continue stress-dose hydrocortisone until the patient is clinically stable and the precipitating cause has resolved or is controlled. In adults, the recommended oral bridge is at least 40 mg hydrocortisone daily in 2 to 4 divided doses or at least 10 mg prednisolone daily in 1 to 2 divided doses before return to the patient's maintenance regimen. [17]

Do not administer fludrocortisone during high-dose hydrocortisone treatment when total hydrocortisone exceeds 50 mg per 24 hours, because hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect at those doses. Reassess mineralocorticoid replacement as hydrocortisone is tapered below this exposure in primary adrenal insufficiency. [3]

For children recovering from adrenal crisis, observe until oral hydrocortisone at sick-day dosing is tolerated. Pediatric sick-day oral hydrocortisone is approximately 30 mg/m2/day in four divided doses, with guidance also describing 30–50 mg/m2/day in three or four doses followed by gradual reduction to maintenance therapy. [1][2]
bullets: Maintain parenteral stress-dose coverage until clinical stability; do not use a fixed laboratory value alone to determine step-down. [17]
Withhold fludrocortisone while hydrocortisone is greater than 50 mg/day. [3]
In pediatric patients, confirm tolerance of oral sick-day hydrocortisone before discharge from acute observation. [2]

table.caption: Glucocorticoid transition decisions after acute adrenal crisis. [1][2][3][17]
rows: Acute adult crisis
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM, then 200 mg/24 hours by infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours. [14][15]
Fludrocortisone is not required when hydrocortisone exceeds 50 mg/24 hours. [3]
Clinically stable adult
Use at least 40 mg/day oral hydrocortisone in 2–4 doses or at least 10 mg/day oral prednisolone in 1–2 doses until the cause resolves and the patient is stable. [17]
Reassess primary adrenal insufficiency mineralocorticoid needs as hydrocortisone is reduced. [3]
Recovering child
Observe until oral sick-day hydrocortisone is tolerated; sick-day dosing is approximately 30 mg/m2/day in four doses or 30–50 mg/m2/day in three or four doses. [1][2]
Individualize ongoing replacement after the stress-dose period. [2]

sections.heading: Identify the precipitant and discharge only with an emergency plan
sections.intro: The episode is incomplete until the trigger and future rescue plan are addressed.
paragraphs: Identify and treat the precipitating cause during admission while maintaining stress-dose glucocorticoid therapy. Continue endocrine team involvement throughout hospitalization to guide etiologic evaluation, replacement adjustment, and safe transition to outpatient care. [17]

Before discharge, ensure that patients with adrenal insufficiency have access to an emergency management kit containing IM hydrocortisone and that the patient or a caregiver can administer it when adrenal crisis is suspected. IM hydrocortisone can be self-administered or administered by nonclinicians in an emergency. [16][17]

For established pediatric adrenal insufficiency, intercurrent illness requiring sick-day treatment should prompt immediate-release oral hydrocortisone in divided doses; children receiving twice-daily modified-release hydrocortisone should be switched to immediate-release hydrocortisone during the sick-day episode. [1]
bullets: Record the precipitant and the glucocorticoid regimen used during the event before discharge. [17]
Provide an injectable hydrocortisone emergency kit and ensure practical administration capability. [16][17]
For illness-related pediatric stress dosing, use immediate-release oral hydrocortisone rather than continuing modified-release hydrocortisone unchanged. [1]

table.caption: Discharge elements that reduce delay in treatment of recurrent adrenal crisis. [1][16][17]
rows: Emergency injection access
Supply an emergency kit containing hydrocortisone for IM injection. [17]
Who may give rescue treatment
Train the patient and caregivers; IM hydrocortisone may be given by the patient, family, or carers when crisis is suspected. [16][17]
Post-crisis specialty follow-up
Arrange endocrine team guidance during and after the admission to define ongoing replacement and evaluate the cause. [17]
Pediatric illness regimen
Use immediate-release oral hydrocortisone in divided sick-day doses; transition from modified-release therapy while unwell. [1]
